mcq.q: A minor borrows ₹40,000 by falsely saying he is an adult. On the lender's suit, the court will hold:
options: The minor is liable for ₹40,000 because of his fraud
The minor is liable once he turns 18
The agreement is voidable at the lender's option
The agreement is void; the minor is not personally liable, though the court may order him to restore benefits still in his hands
mcq.explain: A minor's agreement is void from the beginning (Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose). The rule of estoppel does not apply against a minor, so even a false statement of age does not make him liable. The court may, on equitable grounds, ask him to restore property or money still traceable in his hands.
mcq.topic: Agreements with or by a minor
mcq.fast: Minor = void ab initio. No estoppel, no ratification, no personal liability.

mcq.q: Necessaries suited to his condition in life are supplied to a minor. The supplier can recover the reasonable price:
options: From the minor personally
From the minor's property — Section 68
From the minor's parents personally
Not at all, since the agreement is void
mcq.explain: Section 68 lets a supplier of necessaries to a person who cannot contract, such as a minor, get his money back out of that person's estate. The minor is not personally liable, and parents are not liable unless they authorised the purchase.
mcq.topic: Agreements with or by a minor
mcq.fast: Necessaries to minor -> paid from his PROPERTY, never from him personally.

mcq.q: Hari threatens to burn Sita's shop unless she agrees to sell him her land. Sita agrees. The agreement is:
options: Void
Valid
Voidable at Sita's option, as her consent was caused by coercion
Illegal and punishable
mcq.explain: Threatening to commit an act forbidden by law, such as destroying property, to obtain consent is coercion under Section 15. Section 19 lets the victim of coercion, fraud or misrepresentation choose to avoid the agreement — here the choice is Sita's.
mcq.fast: Coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation -> voidable. Bilateral mistake of fact -> void.

mcq.q: A spiritual guru induces his devotee to gift him her house in return for a promise of "salvation". The contract is:
options: Void for coercion
Valid — gifts are free
Voidable for misrepresentation only
Voidable for undue influence — Section 16
mcq.explain: Section 16 says a person in a position to dominate another's will, such as a spiritual adviser, who misuses that position to gain an unfair benefit is guilty of undue influence. Section 19A gives the influenced party the choice to avoid the contract, and the court may set it aside on just terms.
mcq.fast: Relationship of trust or domination (guru, doctor, guardian) + unfair benefit = undue influence.

mcq.q: Seller knows his horse is unsound but says nothing; the buyer does not ask. The buyer later discovers the defect. Generally:
options: It is fraud — the seller had to disclose
It is coercion
The contract is void for mistake
There is no fraud, as mere silence is not fraud unless there is a duty to speak
mcq.explain: Under the Explanation to Section 17, keeping quiet about facts is generally not fraud. It becomes fraud only where the situation imposes a duty to disclose, or where the silence itself amounts to speaking. In an ordinary sale the seller has no such duty.
mcq.fast: Silence ≠ fraud, EXCEPT duty to speak (fiduciary, insurance, half-truth) or silence = speech.

mcq.q: Both buyer and seller agree to sell a specific cargo which, unknown to both, had already been destroyed at sea. The agreement is:
options: Voidable at the buyer's option
Valid; the seller must pay damages
Valid; the buyer must pay the price
Void — Section 20
mcq.explain: Section 20 makes an agreement void when both sides are mistaken about a fact that is essential to the deal. Here both believed the cargo existed, but it had already perished, so the subject matter did not exist. A unilateral mistake, by contrast, does not make a contract void (Section 22).
mcq.fast: BOTH parties + mistake of FACT + essential = void (s.20). One party only = not void (s.22).

mcq.q: A contract is entered into under a mistake about a law in force in India. The contract is:
options: Void
Voidable
Void if both parties were mistaken
Not voidable — Section 21, ignorance of Indian law is no excuse
mcq.explain: Section 21 states that a contract is not voidable because it was caused by a mistake as to any law in force in India. Everyone is presumed to know the law of the land. A mistake as to a law not in force in India, however, is treated like a mistake of fact.
mcq.fast: Mistake of Indian law = no relief. Foreign law = treated as fact.

mcq.q: An agreement by which a trader promises not to carry on business in a city for 5 years, in return for ₹2 lakh from a rival (no sale of goodwill involved), is:
options: Valid since the restraint is only for 5 years
Valid since consideration was paid
Void — agreement in restraint of trade, Section 27
Voidable at the rival's option
mcq.explain: Section 27 strikes down any agreement that stops a person from carrying on a lawful trade, business or profession. The only statutory exception is for a seller of goodwill, who may promise to stay out of a similar business within a reasonable, defined area. Without a sale of goodwill, the agreement is void.
mcq.fast: Restraint of trade = void, unless the seller of GOODWILL agrees to a reasonable local restraint.

mcq.q: Which agreement is void under Section 26?
options: A promise by an adult never to marry anyone in return for money
A promise by a father not to give consent to his minor daughter's marriage for 2 years
A promise to marry a particular person
A dowry-free marriage agreement between adults
mcq.explain: Section 26 declares void every agreement in restraint of the marriage of any person other than a minor. An adult's promise never to marry restrains marriage and is void. Restraint of a minor's marriage is the exception. A promise to marry a particular person does not restrain marriage at all.
mcq.fast: Restraint of marriage of an ADULT = void (minor is the exception).

mcq.q: Two friends bet ₹5,000 on the result of a cricket match. The loser refuses to pay. The winner:
options: Cannot recover — wagering agreements are void under Section 30
Can recover, as the agreement is valid
Can recover half
Can recover if the bet was in writing
mcq.explain: Section 30 makes agreements by way of wager void, and no suit can be brought to recover anything alleged to be won on a wager. Writing does not save it. The only statutory exception is a subscription or contribution towards a plate, prize or sum of ₹500 or more to the winner of a horse race.
mcq.fast: Bet on an uncertain event = wager = void. Writing does not help.

mcq.q: Under Section 23, which of these makes an agreement's object or consideration unlawful?
options: Opposed to public policy
Inadequate
Paid in advance
Not in writing
mcq.explain: Section 23 names the cases of an unlawful object or consideration: forbidden by law, of such a nature that it would defeat any law, fraudulent, causing harm to someone's person or property, regarded by the court as immoral, or opposed to public policy. Inadequacy, advance payment or lack of writing are not grounds of unlawfulness.
mcq.topic: Legality of object and consideration — Sections 23 and 24
mcq.fast: Section 23 list: forbidden, defeats law, fraudulent, injury, immoral, public policy.
